name: Fluoxymesterone

card.summary: Halotestin: a strong oral androgen from the 1950s that bodybuilders add for hardness and aggression; documented trials are in breast cancer and hypogonadism, none in appearance.
card.note: 17-alpha-alkylated oral androgen; liver and mood effects discussed by forum users and in clinical literature.

quick.overview:
Fluoxymesterone, sold as Halotestin, is an oral androgen first described in the 1950s. In medicine it was used for male hypogonadism and delayed puberty, and as palliative hormone therapy for advanced breast cancer. In bodybuilding and looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a strong, short-acting oral for strength, hardness and aggression rather than for size.

Published trials of the drug are in breast cancer and anemia, not in physique or facial appearance. One looksmax.org poster described planning a regimen with a growth-hormone secretagogue and asked about liver protection.
quick.mechanism: It is a testosterone derivative with a fluorine atom and 17-alpha methyl group that allow oral use and strong androgenic activity; Grokipedia describes it as androgen-receptor mediated with high androgenic potency relative to its anabolic effect.[1][2]
quick.risks: Forum users and one literature summary link long-term use of 17-alpha-alkylated androgens such as fluoxymesterone to hepatocellular adenomas, jaundice and lipid changes, and users describe aggression as a reported effect.[3][4][5] Medical use has declined, and US brand production reportedly ceased in 2014.[1]

lead: Fluoxymesterone (brand names Halotestin and Androxy; also Ultandren and others) is a synthetic oral androgen and anabolic steroid derived from testosterone, taken by mouth. Wikipedia reports it was first described in 1956 and introduced for medical use in the United States in 1957, and a 1957 JAMA note already carried its name.[1][5]

Its medical uses are as androgen replacement for male hypogonadism, for delayed puberty in boys, and as palliative hormone therapy for breast cancer in women; the US Halotestin label lists these indications.[1][4][7] The connection to appearance is through its androgenic and anabolic action: athletes and bodybuilders use androgens to build muscle and strength, and in physique communities fluoxymesterone is discussed as a strong, short-acting oral used for hardness, strength and drive rather than for size.[1][24][23]

Controlled trials of the drug are in oncology and haematology: randomised trials of tamoxifen with or without fluoxymesterone in metastatic breast cancer, the ECOG E3186 chemo-hormonal trial in 231 patients, and a comparison of androgens for anaemia in dialysis patients.[13][9][16][10] No published study has tested it for cosmetic or physique outcomes.

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities users also discuss its documented effects on the liver, blood pressure and mood, and appearance-related androgenic effects such as acne and hair loss; one looksmax.org poster described pairing a low daily amount with the growth-hormone secretagogue MK-677 and asked about liver-support supplements.[19][1][21][22]

chain: Oral androgen acts on androgen receptors in muscle and other tissue
Users report strength and a hard, dense look in training
Claimed improvement in physique, alongside androgenic effects such as acne and hair loss
angle.text: Fluoxymesterone is an androgen, and androgens increase muscle protein synthesis; bodybuilders and strength athletes use it for strength and a hard, dry look rather than for bulk.[2][24][23] These appearance effects are reported by users and have not been tested in published trials of healthy people.[1]

infobox: Male hypogonadism, delayed puberty, palliative breast cancer
US Schedule III; Canada Schedule IV; prohibited in sport

paras: Wikipedia lists male hypogonadism and anaemia in men, delayed puberty, and breast cancer in women as current or past uses; current US prescribing guidance lists male androgen deficiency and female breast cancer.[1] The Halotestin label, produced by Pharmacia and Upjohn, describes replacement therapy for testosterone deficiency including primary and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and delayed puberty in males, and palliation of androgen-responsive recurrent mammary cancer in women who are postmenopausal.[4] A Japanese review groups fluoxymesterone with methyltestosterone as oral androgens used for replacement, and says use in idiopathic male infertility and in erectile dysfunction in elderly men was less effective.[7] Wikipedia notes it is less effective than testosterone at inducing masculinisation but useful for maintaining established masculinisation in adults.[1]
Pediatric literature from 1963 discussed the clinical use and specific dangers of anabolic steroids in children.[6]

Anabolic steroids as a class are used non-medically by athletes, bodybuilders and others to improve physique; Wikipedia's anabolic steroid article estimates that 1 to 3 million people in the United States have used them, mostly non-competitive men with a median age near 25.[3] Wikipedia describes fluoxymesterone use by competitive athletes, bodybuilders and powerlifters to enhance physique and performance.[1] Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference with some promotional material, describes use by power and combat athletes for strength, aggression and muscle hardness.[2]

On looksmax.org, one user describing a plan to ascend again said he intended to take a low daily amount of Halotestin together with MK-677 and asked about timing and liver support.[19] On T Nation, posters describe it as taken before lifting by some strength users and as a compound used for strength gains rather than mass; another says certain anabolic steroids, fluoxymesterone among them, have been used to stimulate growth in short children before growth plates close.[24][25] None of these claims has been tested in a published trial.

Fluoxymesterone is a 17-alpha-alkylated derivative of testosterone carrying a 9-alpha fluorine and an 11-beta hydroxyl group in addition to the 17-alpha methyl group; its formula is C20H29FO3.[1] Wikipedia reports it is a strong androgen with moderate anabolic effects, that it is a substrate for 5-alpha reductase and is converted to 5-alpha-dihydrofluoxymesterone in skin, hair follicles and prostate, and that it is reported not to aromatise to oestrogen because of steric hindrance from the 11-beta hydroxyl, although gynaecomastia has still been reported.[1]

The 17-alpha methyl group blocks first-pass metabolism, giving oral bioavailability of about 80 per cent and a half-life of about 9.2 hours, but also makes the drug hepatotoxic.[1] It binds sex hormone-binding globulin only weakly.[1] Wikipedia also reports it is a potent inhibitor of 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2, an action it describes as unique among anabolic steroids, which may let cortisol activate the mineralocorticoid receptor and has been hypothesised to contribute to hypertension and fluid retention; it has weak affinity for the glucocorticoid receptor.[1] Grokipedia describes the androgen-to-anabolic ratio as roughly 1:1 and notes inconsistent figures.[2] A radioimmunoassay for the drug was published in 1975.[8]

Wikipedia gives 1956 as the year of first description and 1957 as introduction for medical use in the United States.[1] Grokipedia attributes the synthesis to Upjohn chemists and describes clinical adoption for hypogonadism and delayed puberty in the late 1950s and 1960s, expanding palliative breast cancer use, growing liver-toxicity concerns in the 1970s, and restricted prescribing in the 1980s as testosterone products gained favour; these dates come from an AI-generated source.[2]

In the US it was classed as a Schedule III controlled substance and Wikipedia lists it among the few anabolic steroids still available medically, with marketing elsewhere limited to countries such as Mexico, Moldova and Taiwan.[1] Grokipedia reports that the Halotestin brand was discontinued and that production of the Androxy brand halted around 2014; one T Nation poster in 2018 noted that oxandrolone, oxymetholone, fluoxymesterone and methyltestosterone were still on the US market.[2][28]

Human studies of fluoxymesterone are in oncology and haematology. A 1980 controlled trial and a 1988 randomised trial studied tamoxifen alone or combined with fluoxymesterone in postmenopausal women with metastatic breast cancer; a 1983 trial in Annals of Internal Medicine evaluated tamoxifen doses with and without it.[9][13][11] The Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group trial E3186 randomised 231 patients between 1988 and 1992 to chemotherapy or chemotherapy with hormonal therapy, and trial E3185 used a rotating regimen that included Halotestin in 343 patients with hormone-insensitive disease, finding no difference in time to treatment failure between regimens.[16][17] Reviews discuss androgens in adjuvant and metastatic breast cancer therapy.[14][15][12]

A 1981 New England Journal of Medicine study compared androgens, including fluoxymesterone, for anaemia in haemodialysis patients.[10] A registered phase 2 trial of androgen therapy in receptor-negative metastatic breast cancer was terminated after enrolling five patients.[18] No study has tested fluoxymesterone for physique or appearance in healthy people.

Wikipedia lists acne, seborrhoea, alopecia, hirsutism, voice deepening and virilisation; oedema, high blood pressure and cardiovascular toxicity; gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy and prostate enlargement; and increased aggressiveness, suppression of natural testosterone and hepatotoxicity.[1] Wikipedia's anabolic steroid article says liver effects occur mostly or exclusively with 17-alpha-alkylated compounds and lists harmful cholesterol changes, left ventricular hypertrophy and irreversible voice deepening in women and children.[3]

A T Nation poster described oral steroids like Halotestin as having more side effects and liver damage and said jaundice is easy to trigger; another cited literature on prolonged use of methyltestosterone, fluoxymesterone and related androgens showing hepatocellular adenomas that were not uncommon.[21][20] Posters also name it among compounds that can make users aggressive, and describe a flat feeling associated with strong androgens.[22][23] One poster speculated about effects on cortisol metabolism and immune function, citing rodent and in-vitro literature; this was speculation rather than study data, though Wikipedia reports 11-beta-HSD2 inhibition and weak glucocorticoid receptor binding.[27][1]

Wikipedia lists fluoxymesterone as a Schedule III controlled substance in the United States, Schedule IV in Canada and Class C5 in Brazil, and says non-medical use is generally illicit because it is controlled in many countries.[1] It reports that the drug and its metabolites can be detected in urine by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry as used in anti-doping testing.[1] Grokipedia says the World Anti-Doping Agency lists it as prohibited at all times and that the IOC added anabolic steroids to its banned list in 1976 with testing at the Montreal Olympics.[2] A T Nation thread about reference-book warnings in the Physicians' Desk Reference mentions Halotestin among other steroid brands.[29]

Fluoxymesterone is discussed less on looksmax.org than on bodybuilding forums such as T Nation, where it appears in cycle logs, callout threads and training diaries as a potent oral for hardness and drive.[28][22][26] On looksmax.org, the main thread in which it features describes combining it with MK-677 in a plan to ascend again.[19]

timeline.event: Introduced for medical use in the US; JAMA publishes a note on the drug.[1][5]
A pediatrics review discusses the clinical use and specific dangers of anabolic steroids in children.[6]
A radioimmunoassay for fluoxymesterone is published.[8]
A controlled trial compares tamoxifen and fluoxymesterone in advanced breast cancer.[9]
The New England Journal of Medicine publishes a comparison of androgens for anaemia in haemodialysis.[10]
A trial evaluates tamoxifen doses with and without fluoxymesterone.[11]
A randomised trial of tamoxifen alone or with fluoxymesterone in postmenopausal metastatic breast cancer is published; ECOG E3186 enrolment begins.[13][16]
A phase 2 trial of androgen therapy in receptor-negative breast cancer opens and is later terminated with 5 patients.[18]

lore.intro: Halotestin is discussed on forums as a short-acting oral for strength, hardness and drive, with recurring comments on liver toxicity and aggression.[19][23][22]

claims.claim: Halotestin adds hardness and strength more than size
claims.believers: Posters describe a flat, hard feel and strength use, and one describes a user lifting after taking it.[24][23]
claims.experts: No published study has measured physique or strength outcomes of fluoxymesterone in healthy people; the literature is clinical, and Wikipedia describes use by athletes for physique and performance.[13][1]

claims.believers: T Nation members list it among compounds they say are prone to causing aggression.[22]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists increased aggressiveness among its side effects; no published trial examined behaviour in healthy users.[1]

claims.claim: Oral fluoxymesterone is hard on the liver
claims.believers: Users cite jaundice risk and literature on hepatocellular adenomas with prolonged 17-alpha-alkylated steroid use.[20][21]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says the 17-alpha methyl group makes the drug hepatotoxic and that liver effects occur mostly with 17-alpha-alkylated anabolic steroids.[1][3]

claims.claim: Some anabolic steroids, fluoxymesterone included, can promote height gain in short children
claims.believers: A T Nation poster notes use of anabolic steroids to stimulate linear growth in short children before plates fuse.[25]
claims.experts: Pediatric literature reviewed the clinical use and specific dangers of anabolic steroids in children, and Grokipedia notes skeletal monitoring to avoid premature epiphyseal closure when used for delayed puberty; no evidence addresses use for height in healthy teens.[6][2]

claims.claim: A small dose with MK-677 can help someone ascend again
claims.believers: One looksmax.org poster described planning a low daily amount alongside MK-677 and asked about timing and liver protection.[19]
claims.experts: No published study has tested fluoxymesterone with a growth-hormone secretagogue for appearance outcomes.

claims.claim: Fluoxymesterone might affect cortisol and immune function
claims.believers: A T Nation poster raised the idea from rodent and in-vitro literature.[27]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports potent inhibition of 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 and weak glucocorticoid receptor affinity, but human data on immune effects are not described.[1]
